text: The Midas Touch: When Everything Has Only One Kind of Value
Midas began by doing a good deed.
Silenus, the teacher of Bacchus, god of wine, was old and drunk. After losing his way, he was brought to Midas. Midas recognized him, entertained him generously, and personally escorted him back.
Bacchus was delighted and allowed Midas to choose a reward.
Midas said:
Let everything I touch turn to gold.
His wish was fulfilled exactly.

He snapped off a twig: it turned to gold. He picked up a stone: it turned to gold. Clods of earth, ears of grain, apples, doorposts, even the drops of water flowing from his hands flashed gold at his touch.
Midas was beside himself with joy.

What he received was not counterfeit gold, nor an illusion beautiful only from a distance. The power really worked; his wealth really grew. The story did not immediately defeat his wish through some loophole in its wording.
The real failure came at mealtime.
Bread hardened into gold as soon as it touched his hand; meat turned to metal against his teeth. Wine reached his lips as nothing but liquid gold.
Midas sat before a table laden with wealth and began to hunger and thirst.
He possessed ever more valuable things, yet lost the life that made them worth possessing.
This story is often reduced to a single sentence:
Do not be greedy.
That is certainly not wrong. Midas wanted too much, and his wish left no room for anything else.
But greed alone does not explain why the golden touch is so terrifying.
Midas did not simply ask, “Give me more gold.”
He asked that anything coming into contact with him could become nothing but gold.
This goes a step beyond possessing great wealth.

Bread is no longer primarily for eating; water is no longer primarily for quenching thirst. Twigs, stones, and fruit no longer keep their own uses either. Once in Midas's hands, they are converted into the same result.
The problem is not merely that Midas loves gold more than other things.
It is that gold has acquired the authority to say what everything else is worth.
If something can become gold, the change counts as a gain; if it cannot, its original way of existing seems not good enough.
But values are not always interchangeable in this way.

Food has value precisely because it remains food. Drinking water has value because it can enter a body that gets thirsty. Gold can buy food, but once it has replaced food, it cannot carry on doing food's work.
That one thing helps us obtain others does not mean it can therefore replace them.
Only now does Midas discover that, once the means occupies every available place, the end disappears along with everything else.
This prevents the story from becoming “Money has no value.”
Quite the contrary: if gold were truly useless, Midas's wish would not be so enticing.

Wealth can store the fruits of labor, secure resources, cushion unforeseen events, and give a person more choices at important moments. There is nothing shameful in wanting a steadier life, free of the constraints of scarcity.
Midas's problem is not that he sees the value of gold.
It is that he no longer allows other values to exist on their own terms.
When wealth is one force among others in life, it can help people protect their bodies, time, relationships, and future.

When wealth becomes the sole measure of everything, the body becomes merely a cost of maintaining work, time becomes units available for sale, relationships become what they can bring, and even rest must prove that it will yield greater returns later.
Such a person is not simply “too rich.”
He is more like Midas: everything he encounters, he first turns into the same thing, then wonders why life grows ever poorer.
The most frightening thing about the golden touch is not that it produces too much gold.
It is that it leaves nothing in the world that is not gold.
Midas also chose his wish himself.
No one forced him, and no one tricked him by saying gold meant happiness. Bacchus even regretted his choice of such a gift.
This brings the story to a harder question:
Is the fact that a wish is one's own enough to prove that it truly fits one's life?
We often use “I chose this myself” as our final defense.
As long as no one was forced, it seems the consequences need only be borne by that person, and no one else needs to ask further.
But people cannot always see, before choosing, what a wish fully realized will look like.
Some wishes reveal what they take away only after they succeed.

Someone may sincerely want to win, until every relationship becomes a competition; sincerely want recognition, until every action requires spectators; sincerely want security, until no amount of preparation can allow them to start living.
These aims do not become false simply because they are the person's own.
But “It comes from me” and “It is worth my continuing” remain two different questions.
A wish must meet reality before it shows whether it still serves what it originally sought to protect.
Midas was not wholly unfree when he chose.
He merely discovered later that his freedom could also choose a pair of hands that would lock him in.
Once he discovers this, he asks Bacchus to withdraw the gift.
This step matters.
Midas does not say:
Since I chose it, I must see it through to the end.
Nor does he think that, because he has already turned so many things into gold, giving up the power would make everything before look foolish.
He admits he was wrong.
Bacchus tells him to wash the power away at the source of the Pactolus. Midas does so, and the gold leaves his body and enters the river sand.
The story thus does not portray a change of mind as weakness.
What truly enables Midas to live again is not gaining more control, but allowing himself to revoke a choice that has proved destructive to life.
This also reminds us that perseverance is not the highest proof of every freely made choice.
If a wish has begun to swallow what it was meant to serve, remaining loyal to it is not necessarily remaining loyal to oneself.
Sometimes admitting “I truly wanted it once, but now I know I cannot keep wanting it” is how we reclaim the position from which we decide.
Yet why does the golden touch still seem enviable at first?
Because it eliminates the difficulty of conversion.
Others must work, trade, wait, and take risks; Midas only has to touch. The world seems finally to have stopped resisting his wishes. Anything can instantly become the form he values most.
This is another temptation hidden inside the wish:
Not merely to possess wealth, but to have the world stop existing on its own terms.
Bread need not insist on being bread; river water need not insist on being river water. Passing through his hands, they obey the same measure.
But a world that no longer resists us at all can no longer truly sustain us either.
The things we need often have value precisely because they are not extensions of ourselves.

Food has its own properties, land its own conditions, and other people their own needs and answers. We can use, exchange, change, and create, but we cannot treat every difference as a conversion not yet completed.
Midas has gained an absolutely effective power.
The more effective it is, the faster it exposes its poverty: it can do only one thing, and it does not allow the world to refuse.
The story does not ask people to give up wealth.
It merely restores gold to a limited place.
Gold can buy food, but it cannot become food.
It can protect life, but cannot decide on life's behalf what deserves protection.
It can expand our choices, but must not reduce every choice, in the end, to accumulating still more gold.
Midas once believed that turning everything into what was most valuable meant possessing everything.
Only later did he learn that the richness of things lies precisely in their not all being replaceable by a single value.
What the golden touch really took away was not poverty.
It was the world's ability to remain different.
And perhaps this is where wealth most properly belongs:
Helping us approach what wealth cannot replace, without turning those things into itself.

*Textual basis: the Bacchus and Midas episode in Book XI of Ovid's Metamorphoses. This essay follows the continuous account of Midas entertaining and returning Silenus, choosing his reward, turning everything he touches to gold, finding that food and drink also become gold, and washing the power away in the Pactolus. Ovid's passage contains no episode in which Midas turns his daughter into a golden statue; this essay does not use that later popular addition.*
